transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... honestly, it’s getting completely impossible to run my company. I mean, when you're the chief executive, you expect a certain amount of gossip, you know? Office politics, people whispering behind your back, that’s just part of the job and you learn to deal with it. But this is... this is constant, and it's so invasive. 

I keep hearing people talking about me, specifically about me, right through the walls of the main conference room. And it’s not just muffled sounds where you can't make out the words, it’s my board members, or my senior staff, and they are saying horrible things. They keep saying I’m completely ruining the company, that I'm driving the whole operation into the ground. And I hear it from my phone, too. Which is the part I just cannot figure out because I’ll actually power the phone completely down—screen black, totally off, sitting right there on my desk—and their voices still come pouring out of the speaker. 

It sounds so incredibly clear and real that I actually answer them. I’ll speak up and defend my quarterly decisions out loud, or I'll tell them I can hear them and they need to stop, and I'll be halfway through my sentence before I look around and realize... I'm totally alone in the room. Or my assistant is standing in the doorway staring at me, and I realize absolutely no one else heard a single thing. It’s just... how are you supposed to focus on margins and lead a company when your own board is constantly whispering through the electronics and the drywall all day? It's exhausting, it really is.
Have you had a period where you felt unusually energetic or needed much less sleep than usual?

Energetic? God, no. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite right now. I mean, people always assume that when you’re running a company you must be this endless well of energy, you know, the type of person who’s up at 4 AM hitting the treadmill and answering emails before the sun even comes up. And sure, I have my routine, and I work long hours—you have to, it's just the nature of the beast when you're at the top—but I’ve always, always needed a solid seven or eight hours of sleep to actually function properly. Especially when I'm dealing with complex things like our quarterly projections or investor relations. 

But lately... I mean, there is absolutely no burst of energy, no feeling like I just don’t need to sleep. I *want* to sleep. I desperately want to just close my eyes and have it be completely quiet for once. But how are you supposed to get any rest when your own senior staff is practically shouting at you through the bedside lamp? So, yes, I might be awake, I might be lying there at 2 AM just staring a hole into the ceiling, but it is definitely not because I have too much energy. It’s because I’m completely drained, just utterly depleted, and I'm lying there trying to figure out how to protect my company from these people who won't stop talking. So no, I've never had a time where I felt like I didn't need rest... I just can't get any peace to actually take the rest, if that makes sense.
While this has been going on, have you also had a period of feeling very depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say depressed. I mean, sure, I'm stressed. Anyone would be stressed in my position. When you're the chief executive, you're carrying the weight of the entire organization on your shoulders, and that's a heavy burden even on a good day. You've got shareholders breathing down your neck, employees looking to you for direction, and then, on top of all that, you have your own board members constantly undermining you, whispering through the walls, telling you you're ruining everything. It's incredibly stressful. It's frustrating. It makes me angry, honestly, because I've worked so hard to build this company up, to get it to where it is, and they just don't see that. Or maybe they do see it and they're just trying to tear me down out of spite. 

But depressed? Like, sad and crying all day? No, absolutely not. I don't have time to be depressed. I have a company to run. I have to stay sharp, I have to stay focused, even when it feels like the whole world is conspiring against me. I mean, there are moments where I feel completely overwhelmed, where I just want to lock my office door and hide under my desk because the voices are just so loud and so relentless. But that's not depression, that's just... survival, you know? It's self-preservation. I'm trying to protect myself and my company from these people. So no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. Just incredibly, incredibly stressed and exhausted by the whole situation. It's like fighting a war on two fronts—the actual business challenges, and then this constant psychological warfare from my own team. It's just too much sometimes, but I'm not depressed. I'm just trying to hold it all together.
Have you had any recent medical or neurological illness, such as a head injury or seizures?

Medical illness? No. Head injury? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I try to take very good care of myself, physically at least. You have to, right? Like I said, the demands of being a chief executive are just astronomical. You can't afford to be out sick, you can't afford to have a fuzzy head because you bumped it or something. So I'm very careful. I get my annual physicals, my blood work is always perfect—my GP says I have the cholesterol of a twenty-year-old, actually, which is amazing considering the stress I'm under. 

But as far as anything neurological, seizures, head trauma... no, nothing like that. I haven't been in any accidents, I haven't fallen. The only thing that's wrong with my head is that it's constantly being bombarded by these voices from my board members. And I know people might think, "Oh, she's hearing things, she must have a brain tumor," because that's what happens on those medical TV shows, right? Someone starts hearing the radio in their teeth and it turns out to be a massive tumor pressing on their temporal lobe. But I haven't had any headaches—well, aside from tension headaches from the stress of it all, but not, like, medical headaches. No dizzy spells, no passing out, no seizures. My brain is physically completely fine. It's just... it's the environment. It's the technology they're using, or the acoustics of the building, or however they are managing to project their voices into my space. It's an external problem, a personnel problem, really, not a medical one. So, no, physically, neurologically, I am completely healthy. It's just my company that's sick, and they're the ones making it that way.
Have you found yourself becoming much less interested in seeing people or doing things you used to enjoy?

Interested? I mean... I don't know if 'interested' is the right word, but... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly what's happening. It’s actually... it’s really strange, if I’m being completely honest with you. Because I used to be the person driving absolutely every single idea in this company. I mean, I was the engine. If we had a new branch opening or a major launch, I was the one on the phone at ten o'clock at night, calling people right after the openings, getting the immediate feedback, analyzing the numbers, just buzzing with the energy of it all, you know? I thrived on that connection. I absolutely loved my work. It wasn't just a job, it was my entire identity, my passion. 

But now... I don't know what's happened to me. The drive is just gone. Completely gone. I go into my office, and I shut the heavy oak door to try and block out the noise, and I can literally just sit at my desk for hours. Just sitting there in the leather chair, staring at the printed agenda for the day. I don't even really read it. I just stare at the bullet points until they blur into little black lines on the paper, and hours will go by. And I don't do anything. I don't call anyone. I barely even speak to my staff anymore—my executive assistant just leaves folders on the edge of my desk now because she knows I don't want to engage, I don't want to talk. 

And it’s not just at the office, either. It bleeds into everything. I go home and I barely speak to my husband. He tries, you know, he’s a good man, he asks me about my day, asks what we should do for the weekend, and I just... I have absolutely nothing to give him. I don't want to see our friends, I don't want to go to the dinners we used to enjoy. I just don't want to talk to anyone. I just feel... nothing. I look at the quarterly reports, the things that used to get my blood pumping, and I feel almost nothing about the work I used to love so much. It's like all that passion, all that fire that got me to the top in the first place, it just evaporated. I just sit there staring at the paper, feeling completely empty.
Have you found it harder to express your emotions on your face or in your voice lately?

Express my emotions? I... well, it goes right back to what I was just saying, really. How can I express emotions when I don't have any left to express? I mean, think about it. I just told you how I used to be the one driving every single idea, right? Back then, my face, my voice... they were alive. When I was calling people right after those new branch openings, my voice was probably bouncing off the walls. I was animated, I was passionate, I was smiling so much my jaw would hurt by the end of the day. People fed off that energy. I was expressive because I cared so deeply.

But now... now that I feel almost absolutely nothing about this work I used to love so much... my face just kind of matches that nothingness. When I'm sitting at my desk for hours, just staring at that printed agenda like I mentioned, my face is just... blank. It feels heavy, almost like it's made of stone. I don't smile. I don't frown. I just stare. And my voice... on the rare occasions I actually do speak, since I barely speak to my staff or my husband anymore... it just comes out completely flat. Like a dial tone. 

My husband actually asked me the other night if I was furious with him because I sounded so cold, so monotone when I answered a simple question about dinner. But I wasn't mad. I wasn't anything. It’s just that the fire is gone, so there’s no spark left to put into my words or my expressions. I don't have the energy to fake a smile for my assistant, and I don't have the inflection in my voice to pretend I care about the quarterly reports. You can't project warmth or enthusiasm on the outside when you're just feeling completely empty on the inside, you know? It all just feels completely disconnected.
How long have you been hearing these voices?

Three months. It’s been going on for about the past three months now. I mean, I remember when it first started, I genuinely thought there was just a technical issue, like a crossed wire or something with the telecommunications setup in the executive suite. Because at first, it was just coming through my phone. I would be sitting there, and my smartphone would be completely locked, screen totally dark, just sitting there on my desk, and I would hear them. The board members. Whispering about me, criticizing my decisions, right through the speaker of a turned-off phone. 

And I thought, well, maybe it’s a glitch, maybe someone left a secure line open or hacked into the microphone. But then... then it wasn't just the phone anymore. It started coming from the walls. The actual walls of my office. It’s been three solid months of this happening. I even had the building maintenance manager come up during that first month because I was convinced the HVAC system or the acoustics were somehow carrying their conversations from the boardroom directly into my space. They poked around the vents, they tapped on the drywall, and they tried to tell me there was nothing there, no sound carrying over. But I know what I'm hearing. 

It’s been about three months of them using the walls and my phone to project their voices at me, just constantly bombarding my space. Which, like I was saying before, is probably why I just shut down and stare at my desk now. You can't think, you can't lead a company when the walls are literally talking to you with the voices of people trying to undermine you. It's exhausting. But yes, to answer your question, it's been roughly three months of this.
During these past three months, has there been a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices but were not feeling empty or cut off from things?

No, no, they've always... they've been tied together this whole time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. How could I possibly feel anything but completely empty when this has been happening? From the very first week, the very first time I heard them coming through my locked phone—the board members, whispering, plotting—that was when the fire just went out. It was immediate. I remember it so vividly. It was a Tuesday, I had just finished reviewing the Q3 projections, and then... the whispers started. And right then, it was like someone just flipped a switch inside me. 

There hasn't been a single day, let alone two weeks, where I was hearing them but still felt like my old self. How could there be? You can't be the engine of a company, you can't be buzzing with energy and calling people at ten o'clock at night when you know, you absolutely know, that the people you're working for are projecting their voices through the HVAC system to criticize you. The emptiness, the staring at the agenda until the lines blur, the complete inability to talk to my husband or my staff... it all started exactly when the voices started. It’s been three months of both. They are completely intertwined. The voices started, and the passion died. Just like that. There hasn't been any break or any period where one was happening without the other. It's just been three solid months of this heavy, blank nothingness while they whisper at me from the walls.
During these three months, has there been any period of at least two weeks when the voices were still happening but you were not feeling empty or emotionally flat?

I... wait, didn't I just say that? I mean, I'm sorry, I don't mean to be rude, but I feel like I just explained that exact thing. No. The answer is no. There hasn't been a two-week period, or a one-week period, or even a two-day period where the voices were there but I felt fine. 

I just... I don't think you're understanding the timeline here, or maybe I'm just not explaining it right, even though I feel like I am. It's like I was saying about that Tuesday, when I was looking at the Q3 projections. Before that moment, I was me. I was the CEO, I was driven, I was the woman who built this regional division from the ground up. And then the phone started whispering. The locked, dark phone. And the very second that happened, the second I realized the board was monitoring me, criticizing me, projecting their voices into my private office... that was it. The emptiness was immediate. 

It's not like the voices started and then a month later I got depressed or flat or whatever you want to call it. It was instantaneous. The voices started, and the fire went out. So, no, there hasn't been any two-week gap. It's been three months of the voices, and three months of the emptiness, happening at the exact same time, every single day. I just... I don't know how else to explain that they are completely tied together.
Before these last three months began, had you ever heard voices like this at any other time in your life?

No, never. Never in my life. I mean, I'm forty-three years old, and up until three months ago, my mind was... it was a fortress. It was sharp. I built my career on being able to focus, on being the person in the room who could tune out the noise and just get things done. I mean, I didn't finish college, I dropped out because I was already managing a team and making more money than my professors, so I've always trusted my instincts and my mind. 

I've never experienced anything even remotely like this. Not in my twenties when I was working eighty-hour weeks to prove myself, not in my thirties when I took over the regional division... never. There was never a time when I heard things that weren't there, or, well, heard things that other people claim aren't there. I never had voices coming out of my electronics, I never had the walls whispering at me. 

My home, my office, my car... they were all just quiet, normal spaces until that Tuesday three months ago. Before that, the only voices I heard in my office were the ones coming out of the speakerphone when I actually dialed someone. I was completely fine. My head was clear. I was driven. This... this whole nightmare with the board members projecting into my space, this is completely new. It started three months ago, out of nowhere, and it hasn't stopped since. But before that? No. Never. Not once.
About one month after the emptiness and flatness began, were you still hearing the voices?

Yes, absolutely. A month after it all started, the voices were... they were still there. They were relentless. I remember it was right around the time I was supposed to finalize the annual budget, which is usually my favorite time of year, you know? I love diving into the spreadsheets, finding the efficiencies, moving the numbers around until everything clicks into place. It's like a puzzle, and I've always been brilliant at it. But a month in, the emptiness was so heavy, it was like I was moving underwater. I'd sit at my desk, staring at the monitor, just feeling absolutely nothing, no drive, no spark. 

And while I was sitting there, feeling like a ghost in my own office, the voices were still coming through the vents. It was the board members, always the board members. They were whispering about my budget proposals, laughing at my allocations, telling each other I was losing my edge. I could hear them so clearly, even when I felt completely numb to everything else. I tried to focus, I really did, I tried to push through the flatness and just do my job, but they wouldn't stop. They were there a month in, they were there two months in, they're here right now. So yes, to answer your question, a month after the fire went out, the voices were still burning me alive.

doctor.question: Have you found yourself becoming much less interested in seeing people or doing things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the person driving every idea and calling people after openings, but now I can sit at my desk for hours staring at the agenda, barely speak to my husband or staff, and feel almost nothing about work I used to love.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decrease in interest in activities and social interactions, which corresponds to the negative symptoms described in my profile.

patient.answer:
Interested? I mean... I don't know if 'interested' is the right word, but... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly what's happening. It’s actually... it’s really strange, if I’m being completely honest with you. Because I used to be the person driving absolutely every single idea in this company. I mean, I was the engine. If we had a new branch opening or a major launch, I was the one on the phone at ten o'clock at night, calling people right after the openings, getting the immediate feedback, analyzing the numbers, just buzzing with the energy of it all, you know? I thrived on that connection. I absolutely loved my work. It wasn't just a job, it was my entire identity, my passion. 

But now... I don't know what's happened to me. The drive is just gone. Completely gone. I go into my office, and I shut the heavy oak door to try and block out the noise, and I can literally just sit at my desk for hours. Just sitting there in the leather chair, staring at the printed agenda for the day. I don't even really read it. I just stare at the bullet points until they blur into little black lines on the paper, and hours will go by. And I don't do anything. I don't call anyone. I barely even speak to my staff anymore—my executive assistant just leaves folders on the edge of my desk now because she knows I don't want to engage, I don't want to talk. 

And it’s not just at the office, either. It bleeds into everything. I go home and I barely speak to my husband. He tries, you know, he’s a good man, he asks me about my day, asks what we should do for the weekend, and I just... I have absolutely nothing to give him. I don't want to see our friends, I don't want to go to the dinners we used to enjoy. I just don't want to talk to anyone. I just feel... nothing. I look at the quarterly reports, the things that used to get my blood pumping, and I feel almost nothing about the work I used to love so much. It's like all that passion, all that fire that got me to the top in the first place, it just evaporated. I just sit there staring at the paper, feeling completely empty.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are accompanied by prominent negative symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional or brief psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you found it harder to express your emotions on your face or in your voice lately?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the person driving every idea and calling people after openings, but now I can sit at my desk for hours staring at the agenda, barely speak to my husband or staff, and feel almost nothing about work I used to love.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about diminished emotional expression (flat affect), which is a core component of negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Express my emotions? I... well, it goes right back to what I was just saying, really. How can I express emotions when I don't have any left to express? I mean, think about it. I just told you how I used to be the one driving every single idea, right? Back then, my face, my voice... they were alive. When I was calling people right after those new branch openings, my voice was probably bouncing off the walls. I was animated, I was passionate, I was smiling so much my jaw would hurt by the end of the day. People fed off that energy. I was expressive because I cared so deeply.

But now... now that I feel almost absolutely nothing about this work I used to love so much... my face just kind of matches that nothingness. When I'm sitting at my desk for hours, just staring at that printed agenda like I mentioned, my face is just... blank. It feels heavy, almost like it's made of stone. I don't smile. I don't frown. I just stare. And my voice... on the rare occasions I actually do speak, since I barely speak to my staff or my husband anymore... it just comes out completely flat. Like a dial tone. 

My husband actually asked me the other night if I was furious with him because I sounded so cold, so monotone when I answered a simple question about dinner. But I wasn't mad. I wasn't anything. It’s just that the fire is gone, so there’s no spark left to put into my words or my expressions. I don't have the energy to fake a smile for my assistant, and I don't have the inflection in my voice to pretend I care about the quarterly reports. You can't project warmth or enthusiasm on the outside when you're just feeling completely empty on the inside, you know? It all just feels completely disconnected.

inference.note: This turn adds prominent negative symptoms (avolition, social withdrawal, flat affect/alogia-like monotone) alongside persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory content, increasing support for F20.0. Mood episodes remain not clearly syndromal, so F25.9 is less favored but not excluded. F22 is less favored because true auditory hallucinations and negative symptoms are atypical for delusional disorder. No evidence yet to fully rule out acute psychosis duration-wise (F23.3) or organic psychosis (F06.2).

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the psychotic symptoms to distinguish schizophrenia from brief psychotic disorder and delusional disorder/schizoaffective possibilities.
doctor.question: How long have you been hearing these voices?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices from the walls or my phone have been happening for about the past 3 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the duration of the voices (hallucinations), which corresponds to the psychotic symptoms duration.

patient.answer:
Three months. It’s been going on for about the past three months now. I mean, I remember when it first started, I genuinely thought there was just a technical issue, like a crossed wire or something with the telecommunications setup in the executive suite. Because at first, it was just coming through my phone. I would be sitting there, and my smartphone would be completely locked, screen totally dark, just sitting there on my desk, and I would hear them. The board members. Whispering about me, criticizing my decisions, right through the speaker of a turned-off phone. 

And I thought, well, maybe it’s a glitch, maybe someone left a secure line open or hacked into the microphone. But then... then it wasn't just the phone anymore. It started coming from the walls. The actual walls of my office. It’s been three solid months of this happening. I even had the building maintenance manager come up during that first month because I was convinced the HVAC system or the acoustics were somehow carrying their conversations from the boardroom directly into my space. They poked around the vents, they tapped on the drywall, and they tried to tell me there was nothing there, no sound carrying over. But I know what I'm hearing. 

It’s been about three months of them using the walls and my phone to project their voices at me, just constantly bombarding my space. Which, like I was saying before, is probably why I just shut down and stare at my desk now. You can't think, you can't lead a company when the walls are literally talking to you with the voices of people trying to undermine you. It's exhausting. But yes, to answer your question, it's been roughly three months of this.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been at least one month of prominent psychotic symptoms without mood symptoms, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: During these past three months, has there been a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices but were not feeling empty or cut off from things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the temporal relationship between the hallucinations and the negative/mood symptoms (specifically if psychotic symptoms occurred without mood symptoms for at least two weeks, which tests for schizoaffective disorder). My symptom profile does not contain an item addressing this specific temporal relationship.

patient.answer:
No, no, they've always... they've been tied together this whole time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. How could I possibly feel anything but completely empty when this has been happening? From the very first week, the very first time I heard them coming through my locked phone—the board members, whispering, plotting—that was when the fire just went out. It was immediate. I remember it so vividly. It was a Tuesday, I had just finished reviewing the Q3 projections, and then... the whispers started. And right then, it was like someone just flipped a switch inside me. 

There hasn't been a single day, let alone two weeks, where I was hearing them but still felt like my old self. How could there be? You can't be the engine of a company, you can't be buzzing with energy and calling people at ten o'clock at night when you know, you absolutely know, that the people you're working for are projecting their voices through the HVAC system to criticize you. The emptiness, the staring at the agenda until the lines blur, the complete inability to talk to my husband or my staff... it all started exactly when the voices started. It’s been three months of both. They are completely intertwined. The voices started, and the passion died. Just like that. There hasn't been any break or any period where one was happening without the other. It's just been three solid months of this heavy, blank nothingness while they whisper at me from the walls.

inference.note: Voices and negative symptoms/emotional blunting have been present together for 3 months with no 2-week period of psychosis without mood-like symptoms, making F25.9 most likely. Duration >1 month argues against F23.3 but not impossible if course is still evolving. Lack of medical/neurological history lowers F06.2; prominent hallucinations exclude pure delusional disorder F22.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least one month in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: During these three months, has there been any period of at least two weeks when the voices were still happening but you were not feeling empty or emotionally flat?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the temporal relationship between psychotic symptoms and mood/negative symptoms (specifically looking for a 2-week period of psychosis without mood symptoms to rule out schizoaffective disorder), which is not explicitly covered by any single item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I... wait, didn't I just say that? I mean, I'm sorry, I don't mean to be rude, but I feel like I just explained that exact thing. No. The answer is no. There hasn't been a two-week period, or a one-week period, or even a two-day period where the voices were there but I felt fine. 

I just... I don't think you're understanding the timeline here, or maybe I'm just not explaining it right, even though I feel like I am. It's like I was saying about that Tuesday, when I was looking at the Q3 projections. Before that moment, I was me. I was the CEO, I was driven, I was the woman who built this regional division from the ground up. And then the phone started whispering. The locked, dark phone. And the very second that happened, the second I realized the board was monitoring me, criticizing me, projecting their voices into my private office... that was it. The emptiness was immediate. 

It's not like the voices started and then a month later I got depressed or flat or whatever you want to call it. It was instantaneous. The voices started, and the fire went out. So, no, there hasn't been any two-week gap. It's been three months of the voices, and three months of the emptiness, happening at the exact same time, every single day. I just... I don't know how else to explain that they are completely tied together.

inference.note: Changed F25.9 to F25.1 because psychotic symptoms and persistent depressive/negative symptoms have been concurrent for the full 3 months with no at least 2-week period of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms, arguing against schizophrenia and supporting depressive-type schizoaffective disorder. F23.3 remains possible given total duration under 3 months, though less favored if symptoms persist beyond 3 months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a sustained period of psychotic symptoms without prominent negative or mood symptoms, which would distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and acute polymorphic psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Before these last three months began, had you ever heard voices like this at any other time in your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's past psychiatric history, specifically if they have ever experienced auditory hallucinations prior to the current 3-month episode. This information is not covered in the provided symptom profiles, which only detail the current symptoms and their duration.

patient.answer:
No, never. Never in my life. I mean, I'm forty-three years old, and up until three months ago, my mind was... it was a fortress. It was sharp. I built my career on being able to focus, on being the person in the room who could tune out the noise and just get things done. I mean, I didn't finish college, I dropped out because I was already managing a team and making more money than my professors, so I've always trusted my instincts and my mind. 

I've never experienced anything even remotely like this. Not in my twenties when I was working eighty-hour weeks to prove myself, not in my thirties when I took over the regional division... never. There was never a time when I heard things that weren't there, or, well, heard things that other people claim aren't there. I never had voices coming out of my electronics, I never had the walls whispering at me. 

My home, my office, my car... they were all just quiet, normal spaces until that Tuesday three months ago. Before that, the only voices I heard in my office were the ones coming out of the speakerphone when I actually dialed someone. I was completely fine. My head was clear. I was driven. This... this whole nightmare with the board members projecting into my space, this is completely new. It started three months ago, out of nowhere, and it hasn't stopped since. But before that? No. Never. Not once.

inference.note: No prior lifetime psychosis supports first-episode illness; persistent auditory hallucinations with concurrent negative/depressive symptoms for 3 months and no 2-week psychosis-only period argues against F20.0 and keeps schizoaffective depressive type vs acute psychotic disorder with associated depressive symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least one month after the onset of negative symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia over acute polymorphic psychotic disorder with symptoms of schizophrenia.
doctor.question: About one month after the emptiness and flatness began, were you still hearing the voices?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the relative timeline/overlap of the negative symptoms (emptiness/flatness) and the hallucinations (voices) at a specific point in time (one month after emptiness began). This relates to the chronological relationship between psychotic and mood/negative symptoms (often used to differentiate schizoaffective disorder or major depressive disorder with psychotic features), which is not explicitly covered by a single symptom profile item in the provided list. The 'psychotic_symptoms_duration' covers the 3-month duration of voices, but doesn't specifically address this cross-symptom timeline question.

patient.answer:
Yes, absolutely. A month after it all started, the voices were... they were still there. They were relentless. I remember it was right around the time I was supposed to finalize the annual budget, which is usually my favorite time of year, you know? I love diving into the spreadsheets, finding the efficiencies, moving the numbers around until everything clicks into place. It's like a puzzle, and I've always been brilliant at it. But a month in, the emptiness was so heavy, it was like I was moving underwater. I'd sit at my desk, staring at the monitor, just feeling absolutely nothing, no drive, no spark. 

And while I was sitting there, feeling like a ghost in my own office, the voices were still coming through the vents. It was the board members, always the board members. They were whispering about my budget proposals, laughing at my allocations, telling each other I was losing my edge. I could hear them so clearly, even when I felt completely numb to everything else. I tried to focus, I really did, I tried to push through the flatness and just do my job, but they wouldn't stop. They were there a month in, they were there two months in, they're here right now. So yes, to answer your question, a month after the fire went out, the voices were still burning me alive.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms have persisted for 3 months with prominent negative symptoms (affective flattening, avolition, social withdrawal) beginning with the psychosis. There has been no mood episode meeting criteria for mania or major depression, ruling against F25.1. Duration >1 month rules out F23.3.

opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusional interpretations lasting 3 months, along with prominent negative symptoms (avolition, social withdrawal, affective flattening, alogia-like reduction in speech, anhedonia/emptiness). Mood episodes were denied as primary syndromes: no manic episode and no major depressive syndrome endorsed; psychotic symptoms were not present outside the same period as the negative symptoms, and there is no medical/neurological explanation elicited. The pattern is most consistent with schizophrenia, catatonic type not supported, disorganized type not described, making F20.2 the best match among provided candidates.
